body.text: Attribution: Vinayak Sharma and D.C.S. Mayal, “Soft Power with Sharp Edges: China’s Global Narrative War,” ORF Occasional Paper No. 579, Observer Research Foundation, November 2026.

Chinese cultural traditions have a profound influence on the People’s Republic of China’s (PRC) strategic outlook. Beijing considers itself the natural inheritor of the world, owing to its Tianxia (All under Heaven) philosophy.[1] Tianxia underpins the Communist Party of China’s (CCP) strategic worldview, conceptualising a hierarchical order with China at its civilisational centre. It is a concept rooted in Confucian principles. At the centre stands a ruler whose authority derives from the Mandate of Heaven, which has been granted based on moral virtue rather than the notion of ‘Divine Right.’

This broad civilisational worldview is complemented by the concept of Zhongguo (Middle Kingdom). This is how imperial China described itself—the ‘civilised’ centre of the world and the link between heaven and earth, reinforcing the perception of China as the natural centre of political and cultural authority.[2] Zhongguo represents the geographical and cultural manifestation of the Tianxia order, supporting the belief that China occupies a naturally central and superior position in the international hierarchy.

However, this deeply embedded self-perception was severely disrupted during the period commonly referred to as the ‘century of humiliation.’[3] This began in 1839 with the Chinese defeat at the hands of the British in the First Opium War (1839–42) and ended in 1949 with the establishment of the PRC following the conclusion of the Second World War and the Communists taking over the country. The memory of this ‘century of humiliation’ forms the framework, in modern times, of Beijing’s interaction with the world. China is working assiduously to establish a global order where that memory—characterised by constant defeats, political fragmentation, and the subjugation of the Qing Dynasty and the Republic of China (the PRC’s predecessor government) by foreign powers (several West European countries, Russia, and Japan)—becomes part of the forgotten past.[4],[5]

All of the CCP’s actions, whether for territorial expansion or economic gain or any other advance, are aimed at achieving this greater goal.[6] China wants to become the world’s sole superpower.[7] It is competing with the United States (US) on various fronts, particularly trade. There is also indirect territorial competition as the US, without making any direct claim on the South China Sea (SCS), seeks to expand its influence there through its allied nations in the region, which China strongly resists. Regarding Taiwan too, there is a tussle as the US, while acknowledging China’s non-negotiable ‘One China’ position (which insists that Taiwan is an integral part of the PRC), supports maintaining the status quo (whereby Taiwan is actually a separate nation) and bolsters Taiwan’s defence capabilities.[8] The competition also extends to the information domain, where China has leveraged its economy to prevent any rhetoric against Chinese goals from reaching its people. Be it entertainment, news television, social media, or even academic discourse, all such content has been systematically smothered while media seen as promoting national goals has been given space to flourish.

The concept of ‘soft power,’ originally coined by Harvard academic Joseph Nye, refers to the “ability of a country to attract others because of its culture, political values, and foreign policy.”[9] The cornerstone of Nye’s assertion is that in modern global politics, the tools of attraction (such as media) are just as important as those of coercion (such as military). This makes soft power a crucial tool for long-term influence-building. While soft power focuses on attraction, there is a closely related concept of ‘sharp power’ that focuses on subtle coercion through censorship, manipulation, and information warfare.[10] China combines soft and sharp power to effectively advance its propaganda objectives among targeted audiences. The ‘soft’ aspect includes the circulation of film media and the ‘sharp’ encompasses censorship, both of which have been analysed later in this paper.

China has leveraged the allure of its soft power to disseminate its message to the masses with such effectiveness that quoting the fifth-century BCE Chinese general Sun Tzu’s Art of War has become a trend in Hollywood. The Art of War has even been quoted in non-war media—films such as Wall Street and Die Another Day, and TV series such as The Sopranos and Star Trek: The Next Generation. This may appear trivial, but it points to a trend of Chinese culture becoming much more visible than before and getting a more advantageous position in Western public perception battle than other competing cultures.

This paper seeks to highlight the steps taken by China to expand its soft power apparatus in pursuit of its superpower goal. It focuses on the institutional measures taken by the Chinese government in multilateral fora, its media manipulation, and restrictions in the academic field—all intended to establish Pax Sinica (Chinese Peace). ‘Pax’ comes from Latin, meaning ‘peace,’ and has been used in past instances as well, in conjunction with the dominant global power, to denote a relative period of peace enforced by the said power.

China’s international dealings, since the Mao Zedong period ended with his death in 1976, can be clubbed into two groups: pre- and post-Deng Xiaoping, the former paramount leader of China from 1978 to 1989. Deng’s now-famous dictum “Hide your strength, bide your time” has been Beijing’s state policy, whereby it follows a strategy of muted diplomacy and strategic statesmanship.[11] Following Deng’s ascendance, China’s gross domestic product (GDP) underwent a radical change over the next two decades, rising more than sixfold from around US$150 billion in 1978 to US$968 billion in 1997.[12]

With economic growth, China ensured that its global impact increased as well. In 1995, for instance, when Taiwan made a push for international recognition as a separate nation and its then President Lee Teng-hui was invited to the US, China responded by firing missiles across the Taiwan Strait.[13] It has since continued this policy of initiating asymmetric hostilities in response to actions it deems inimical to its perception/goals. In 2013, it began building entire artificial islands on coral reefs in the SCS to expand its maritime borders, to which the Philippines protested by instituting arbitral proceedings at the Permanent Court of Arbitration at the Hague against China for violating the United Nations (UN) Convention on the Law of the Sea.[14] In 2016, the Hague tribunal agreed that China had indeed violated the Philippines’ sovereign rights in those waters by interfering with its fishing and petroleum exploration and constructing artificial islands.[15] But Beijing did not recognise the Court’s jurisdiction and chose not to participate in the proceedings.[16] China’s growing temerity is clear: in 1995, after its missile strike at Taiwan, it was still sufficiently bothered about global opinion to send a diplomatic mission to the US to clarify that it had no intention of invading Taiwan. By 2016 it was openly rejecting the verdict of an international organisation. While these are vastly different scenarios that should not equated, this indicates a change in the conduct of international relations.

However, China does not always ignore international organisations; it recognises their value too. It increasingly views the United Nations (UN) as a strategic stage to advance its long-term national interests and redesign global governance in line with its ‘Middle Kingdom’ vision. Since joining the UN in 1971, it has meticulously expanded its influence by placing nationals and proxies in key positions, directing substantial funding, and launching development programmes aligned with its agenda. Notably, China led four of the UN’s 15 specialised agencies in 2020, the most by a single country. This influence has enabled China to promote its leading companies like telecom giant Huawei through bodies such as the International Telecommunication Union, implant favourable standards, and steer discussions away from sensitive topics such as human rights.[17] Former UN whistleblower Emma Reilly uncovered proof of China influencing the reports of UN bodies such as the Office of the High Commissioner of Human Rights (OHCHR), making them not raise certain issues relating to its human rights record.[18]

China now contributes approximately 20 percent of the UN’s regular budget and nearly 23 percent of its peacekeeping costs—a dramatic increase from less than 1 percent in 1994—positioning it as the second-largest financial contributor to the UN after the US.[19] This financial influence, coupled with procedural assertiveness, enables it to shape agendas, silence criticism, and build coalitions to confront the traditional rules-based international order. Over the last two decades, ever since it entered the World Trade Organisation (WTO) in 2001, China has set out to influence the global multilateral system. In 2002, it established the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO), which made the US recognise the threat of an emerging China. Both institutions are utilised by Beijing as two parallel tracks to achieve its goals—the WTO for global economic integration and the SCO for regional economic consolidation.[20] Indeed, SCO members, including China, have affirmed their commitment to a “WTO-centred multilateral trading system.”[21] Beijing uses the organisation to shape trade geography that ultimately operates under WTO rules.[22]

After the 11 September 2001 attacks in the US, America’s military and economic apparatus focused on the ‘War on Terror,’ allowing China to grow further in the shadows.[23] In other cases, the US ceded influence wilfully. In June 2018, during President Donald Trump’s first term, Washington left the UN Human Rights Council (UNHRC), accusing it of “unending hostility towards Israel,”[24] which, in practice, allowed China to exert more influence in the UNHRC than before.

As China’s economic and multilateral heft has grown, many countries that are not traditional regional powers have begun diplomatically leveraging their interests by voting in consonance with Beijing’s wishes. This advantage is further reinforced by the numerous high-level positions held by Chinese representatives, which contributes to the failure of resolutions critical of Beijing to secure sufficient support Take, for instance, the draft resolution submitted against China at the UNHRC[25] in September 2022, following the widespread international condemnation of the internment of Muslims in Xinjiang Province. It was signed by the US, Canada, Denmark, Finland, Iceland, Norway, and Sweden, while the UK proposed a discussion on the human rights situation in Xinjiang at the next UNHRC’s next session.[26] The resolution was rejected following 17 votes in favour, 19 against, and 11 abstentions.[27] The nations that voted against included Pakistan, Nepal, and Kazakhstan (among others), which are also countries with a vested interest in maintaining a positive relationship with China.

It is such influence that makes China impervious to any global pressure exerted upon it to toe the line of the international community. Such pressure should not be underestimated; among other factors, it resulted in the dismantling of the apartheid regime in South Africa.[28]

China’s growing influence within international institutions is not limited to procedural power or financial leverage. It also seeks to shape the very language, norms, and conceptual frameworks through which global governance is understood. Its strategies encompass systematic discursive leadership and a deliberate redefinition of global norms and institutional language to advance its strategic vision of Pax Sinica. Projects such as its Belt and Road Initiative (BRI) and its slogan of “community of shared future for mankind” have increasingly been incorporated into official UN discourse,[29] reflecting China’s transition from passive institutional participation to active norm-shaping. This shift represents the essence of China’s huayuquan (discourse power), where it does not merely engage with existing international norms but actively rewrites them to align with the CCP’s interests and authoritarian governance model. This discursive transformation is now also operationalised through China’s recently launched Four Global Initiatives (4GIs)—the Global Development Initiative (GDI), Global Security Initiative (GSI), Global Civilisation Initiative (GCI), and the Global Governance Initiative (GGI). Launched between 2021 and 2025, these represent a bold advancement in Chinese statecraft, fusing public diplomacy, governance reform, and uniquely scaled mass human intelligence networks to reshape the global order, while avoiding any direct confrontation or raising red flags.

As the US’s global leadership retreats under Trump, Beijing is exploiting the resulting vacuum by infiltrating existing international organisations and creating new ones to shape nascent domains such as artificial intelligence (AI), space, and deep-sea mining. The GGI, framed as South–South solidarity, is cultivating Global South dependencies, implanting pervasive intelligence networks, and universalising Chinese norms, gradually displacing Western paradigms and challenging institutional transparency.[30] This integrated narrative architecture positions Beijing as the ideological alternative to Western-led globalisation, embedding terminology such as “shared future,” “win-win cooperation,” and “multi-polarity” into international institutions and diplomatic language. China’s Confucius Institutes (CI) serve as nodes in this discursive-intelligence network, synchronising cultural outreach with efforts to manipulate academic databases, influence international media narratives, and suppress dissenting views. The convergence of soft power instruments with discursive leadership and the 4GIs is enabling China to reshape global governance from within and normalise Pax Sinica as ‘inclusive’ multilateralism, while advancing its strategic objectives under the garb of global public goods.[31]

The United Front Work Department (UFWD) serves as the CCP’s nerve centre for global influence operations. It has been expanded significantly by President Xi Jinping to strengthen party leadership, spread ideology, and ensure China’s global rejuvenation through systematic co-opting of overseas Chinese populations. The UFWD directs ‘overseas Chinese work’ by leveraging elite-to-elite diplomacy, where officials and agents in diplomatic roles build relationships with foreign politicians and influential overseas Chinese to shape policies, undermine opposition, and promote CCP interests globally.[32] Leaked documents reveal that Chinese authorities utilise students in BRI countries through UFWD-managed associations, which oversee 42 local organisations and have 220,000 members abroad.[33] The Chinese Students and Scholars Association (CSSA), the largest UFWD-affiliated organisation for overseas Chinese students, operates under the cloak of spreading Chinese culture, while monitoring the thoughts and behaviours of Chinese students in foreign universities, limiting academic freedom, prescribing correct speech, harassing anti-China speakers, and ensuring that students remain patriotic and supportive of the CCP’s rule. There is also the China Association for International Friendly Contact (CAIFC), which collects intelligence across 70 countries under the cover of friendly exchanges.[34]

The UFWD uses scholarships to attract international students (two-thirds from BRI nations) while the CSSA recruits party members and promotes self-censorship among students through the implied threat of losing scholarships or facing harassment. In 2018, China’s State Administration for Religious Affairs was restructured under the UFWD, expanding Buddhist diplomacy to bolster the BRI’s cultural mission and enhance soft power across Southeast Asia. The UFWD collaborates with the Ministry of State Security (MSS) to suppress Chinese critics, coordinates propaganda targeting diaspora communities, and oversees strategic acquisition of overseas media outlets under the guidance of the Central Propaganda Department (CPD), transforming educational diplomacy and religious outreach into systematic political control networks.[35]

Beyond formal institutions, China’s influence strategy increasingly extends into the global information ecosystem. Beijing has invested heavily in projecting its soft power, leveraging its population size and economic might to either set the narrative or capture discourse spaces to serve its strategic interests. One of the many ways is through international media. It invests billions annually in global information manipulation, using propaganda, disinformation, and censorship to promote CCP narratives, while suppressing criticism of its human rights record, its position on Taiwan, and its SCS claims. Beijing maximises pro-PRC content through foreign media stakes, sponsored influencers, and restrictive content-sharing agreements disguising state propaganda as legitimate local news. Coercive tactics include online/offline intimidation, corporate retaliation, legal actions against critics in democracies, and WeChat technical censorship targeting overseas Chinese communities with harvested data.[36]

In 2009, the CCP approved investing close to 45 billion Yuan (US$6.3 million) in buying media real estate.[37] A 2018 Bloomberg report has outlined how Beijing systematically inveigled itself into the European media industry by investing more than US$2 billion since 2008.[38] According to a filing under the US’s Foreign Agents Registration Act (FARA), China Daily, a Beijing-based CCP-run media house, provided funds under various guises such as operational costs (taxes, payroll, administration rent expenses, and more) and advertising revenue, among others, to prominent media houses in the US,[39] including The Washington Post (US$4.6 million), The Wall Street Journal (WSJ) (US$6 million), The Los Angeles Times (US$110,000), The Houston Chronicle (US$92,000), and The Boston Globe (US$76,000).[40] Among these, by 2020, WSJ was found to have carried the most extensive amount of CCP propaganda, such as a daily insert titled ‘China Watch,’ which presented pro-China news, focusing on its economy, culture, and geopolitics. Since this became public knowledge, WSJ has acknowledged that it is a ‘paid programme’ by China Daily and maintains that the paper is not involved in its content.[41]

Such investments effectively buy China control over media editorial policies which, in turn, results in the highlighting of China-related stories the way Beijing wants them, suppressing those it deems anti-China, or running a counter narrative.[42] A blatant example was the New York Times story of 4 January 2021, during the COVID-19 pandemic, titled ‘In a Topsy-Turvy Pandemic World, China Offers Its Version of Freedom’ that claimed: “Surveillance and censorship bolster Beijing’s uncompromising grip on power. But in the country’s cities and streets, people have resumed normal lives.”[43] The report, justifying Chinese news censorship, had political commentators accusing NYT of “shilling for communist China.”[44]

Beijing’s largest investment in the US communications industry may not be in the news media but in the movies. Chinese entertainment group Dalian Wanda bought the US cinema chain AMC Entertainment for US$2.6 billion in May 2012,[45] following it up by acquiring Legendary Entertainment, another mass media company, for US$3.5 billion, in January 2016.[46] Simultaneously, the Chinese movie market has become increasingly important for US producers, with the number of movie screens in China exceeding those in the US by 2017. This has given China enormous influence in Hollywood, which has begun tailoring its casting, stories, and business choices to Chinese audience tastes. Producers are pressured to portray China and Chinese characters in a positive light or risk losing the largest movie-going audience in the world.

The trailer of the film Top Gun: Maverick (2022), for instance, originally intended to show the titular character sporting the Taiwanese and Japanese flags on his jacket. In the final cut, the flags were removed, keeping in mind that one of the film’s financiers was Tencent, a Chinese multinational technology conglomerate. They were restored in the actual movie, though, after Tencent left the project.[47] Another film, Doctor Strange (2016), changed the nationality of one of the major characters who in the source material had been Tibetan, reportedly to avoid annoying the Chinese.[48] The film Pixels (2015) deleted a scene which depicted the Great Wall being destroyed, once again following Chinese pressure; the final cut showed India’s Taj Mahal being blown up instead.

It was in the 1990s that Hollywood first learnt of the CCP’s red lines. The film Seven Years in Tibet (1997), which portrayed the Chinese incorporation of Tibet in a largely critical light,[49] enraged Chinese censors so much that Beijing threatened to disrupt the distributor Sony’s supply chain in China, which would have cost billions to rebuild.[50] It was a time when the 14th Dalai Lama’s fame had skyrocketed, due to actors like Richard Gere and musicians like Tina Turner and the Beastie Boys supporting the ‘Free Tibet’ cause.[51] Eventually, it was the likes of Gere who suffered—his activism in favour of Tibetan freedom led to him being exiled, first from the Academy Awards, and later, effectively, from Hollywood itself.[52] Similarly, another movie, the Martin Scorsese-directed Kundun produced by Disney, also released in 1997, which tells the story of the Dalai Lama in the backdrop of the People’s Liberation Army’s (PLA) invasion of Tibet, the threat to his life, and his subsequent forced exile to India, saw Beijing threatening to cancel Disney’s access to the Chinese market. Disney capitulated, quietly strangling the film by minimising its marketing budget and even curtailing its US release, assuaging the Chinese by stating that “very few had seen Kundun.”[53]

The importance of the Chinese market for Hollywood is underlined by the fate of yet another movie, Black Panther (2018), part of the Marvel Cinematic Universe (MCU), which had a black actor, Chadwick Boseman, a first for the MCU. Yet this progressive aspect of the film was obscured in its China release, where Boseman’s face was covered by a mask, apparently because the Chinese audience did not like blacks in lead roles.[54] From 2019–22, no Marvel movie was allowed into China, without any official explanation, though many suspect it could be due to comments critical of China made by some of the people involved in the films.[55] Another comic-book movie, Black Adam, was also denied a China release, presumably because it starred Pierce Brosnan, who had previously shared a picture of himself with the Dalai Lama.[56]

On social media, China has set a blanket ban on all popular foreign-based apps such as Facebook, Google, Instagram, LinkedIn, Messenger, Reddit, Telegram, Vimeo, WhatsApp, X, Yahoo, and YouTube, commonly referred to as the ‘Great Firewall.’[57] What is fascinating is that even TikTok, owned by Beijing-based ByteDance, is banned in China, though its original version, called Douyin, is allowed. Both Douyin and TikTok share the same interface and underlying technology, but operate on separate networks and content is not shared between them. While TikTok prioritises global entertainment and music based on its ability to go ‘viral,’ Douyin is heavily curated by the Chinese government to promote ‘pro-social’ content, prioritising patriotism, science experiments, and educational videos. Douyin users are also generally older than those of TikTok; it has a ‘youth mode’ that limits users under 14 years of age to 40 minutes per day, in addition to locking them out completely between 10 p.m. and 6 a.m.[58] In 2021, China overhauled its digital laws to limit the time children spent online on social media and video gaming.[59] The difference in content curation by the two subsidiaries clearly points to the social engineering China practises through media platforms and shows how digital ecosystems can be calibrated to shape social behaviour and political attitudes.

The main organisations controlling the media in China are the Central Propaganda Department (CPD) of the CCP,[60] the National Radio and Television Administration (NRTA),[61] the Cyberspace Administration of China (CAC),[62] the Ministry of State Security (MSS), the Ministry of Public Security (MPS),[63] and the State Council Information Office (SCIO).[64] The CPD sets the ideological tone for all media content and issues daily directives to media outlets. The NRTA, formerly known as the State Administration of Press, Publication, Radio, Film, and Television (SAPPRFT), regulates broadcast content (TV, radio, streaming platforms), issues licences, and monitors compliance with propaganda guidelines.[65] The CAC regulates online content and the internet; manages censorship of websites, social media platforms, and search engines; enforces China’s strict internet laws; and controls data flow.[66] The SCIO functions as the CPD’s face, hosting press conferences and publishing white papers to shape China’s international perception.[67] The MSS and MPS monitor both domestic and foreign journalists/media personnel and enforce the law.

China mainly uses the China Global Television Network (CGTN), China Central Television (CCTV), Xinhua TV, China Radio International (CRI), print media such as China Daily Global Weekly or China Daily Global Edition, and several Chinese state-run media bureaus such as Xinhua News Agency and China Daily to exercise control. CGTN is broadcast in 140 countries and CRI in 65 languages.[68] In 2020, CGTN claimed that it broadcast to 1.2 billion people globally, in Chinese, English and other languages;[69] though that figure was inflated, the real numbers, according to the Lowy Institute, are close to 50 million, far from insubstantial.[70] In March 2018, CGTN, CCTV, and CRI were merged under a new parent organisation, China Media Group.

Beijing has also expanded its global media presence through a vast network of foreign bureaus operated by its state-run outlets. The bureaus disseminate Chinese narratives and exert media influence worldwide, enabling Beijing to project favourable narratives while contesting Western information dominance. Xinhua employs approximately 12,000 staff and operates a global network comprising 182 overseas bureaus, including seven regional offices. It publishes more than 20 newspapers and magazines, delivers news services in seven languages, and provides multimedia news content in eight countries.[71] CGTN, China Daily, CRI, Xinhua, and CNS all operate expansive digital and social media platforms, broadcasting in more than 12 languages worldwide. Xinhua has dramatically expanded its global footprint, opening 40 new foreign bureaus between 2009 and 2011, and by August 2021, it had 181 bureaus across 142 countries.

The CCP’s International Liaison Department maintains relationships with over 600 political entities across more than 160 countries, amplifying Beijing’s diplomatic influence. While some of his predecessors adopted relatively more liberal approaches, under Xi Jinping, the ‘party media’ principle—absolute party control over media—has become sacrosanct, with the CPD directly overseeing the China Media Group, ensuring unified messaging domestically and abroad.[72] A long-term study by scholars Hannah Waight et al. revealed that on 90 percent of the days between 2012 and 2022, over 80 percent of party newspapers included content sent out by the CPD in their columns; on important days, such as during Party Congresses, 30–58 percent of newspaper content comprised such material. The study also noted that under Xi Jinping, CPD-provided articles on newspapers’ front pages tripled from 5 to 6.7 percent in 2012 to 20.3 percent in 2021, with overall propaganda rising proportionally from 6.1 percent to 7.8 percent. Many newspapers were found to have used the CPD-provided content verbatim, without even bothering to tweak the language.[73]

Even non-party commercial papers averaged 2–4 percent scripted content with identical spikes, debunking claims that commercialisation had made Chinese media more independent. CPD-issued scripts extend beyond ideology to policy, diplomacy, and even coverage of crises; over 50 percent of the coverage of severe earthquakes in China, it was found, was CPD-scripted. So too was the COVID-19 pandemic coverage: though the first cases in China were noticed by late November 2019, before the Wuhan lockdown on 23 January 2020, less than 50 articles on the pandemic had appeared in the Chinese press and nearly all of them were CPD-scripted; post lockdown, however, coverage exploded to 10,000–15,000 daily articles, but the ‘scripting’ continued.[74]

The ‘smart cities/safe cities’ surveillance technologies that China exports to several countries in Africa, Latin America, and parts of Asia also enables authoritarian digital norms, which the recipient nations rapidly adopt. Unchecked, these can create pro-Beijing information channels, enable surgical targeting powered by AI, and produce multilateral amplification of CCP narratives, distorting sovereign decision-making worldwide.[75] On social media platforms, China extensively employs bots and trolls; Twitter (now X), for instance, shut down more than 1,70,000 pro-China accounts[76] and more than 28,000 multi-channel networks (MCNs) by 2020 that disseminated Beijing’s narratives using ethnic minority influencers on YouTube.[77]

In the last decade, responding to the technological revolution, China has enacted new laws providing legal cover for media manipulation. These include the Data Security Law (September 2021) and Personal Information Protection Law (November 2021) for data surveillance/censorship; the 2025 MCN Regulations forcing influencers to follow CCP ‘political direction’ and banning ‘rumours;’ the 2025 AI Content Labelling Rules to combat ‘fake news’ through mandatory disclosure; and the Cyber Security Law Amendment (January 2026) tightening AI/content controls.[78]

In the field of culture, China began the CI programme in 2004 to—as its website claims—promote Chinese language and culture, engage in educational cooperation, and facilitate people-to-people exchanges with other nations. The website further claims that the programme operates upon the principles of mutual respect, friendly consultation, equality, and mutual benefit.[79] Jointly established by Chinese and local partner organisations, as of 2017, there were 516 CIs across the world, while another 1,076 Confucius Classrooms (CCs) partnered with local schools globally.[80] These establishments range from primary and secondary schools to the college and university level, with a presence in 146 countries, including an estimated 100–120 (gauged from 173 in Europe before the 2025 closures) in the member states of the North Atlantic Treaty Organization (NATO).[81],[82]

The CI model has been described as a ‘soft power success’ by NATO’s Strategic Communications Centre of Excellence.[83] In practice, CIs allow the CCP to assert undue influence by propagating only those concepts that toe its line and pressure institutes in other countries to exclude those narratives it opposes. In March 2008, for example, Tel Aviv University in Israel shut down an exhibition by the Falun Gong, the Chinese spiritual discipline based on Buddhist and Taoist thought touted as ‘heretical’ by the CCP.[84] An Israeli court later found that the university had illegally cancelled the exhibition because of CI’s pressure. Furthermore, a Canadian Coalition on Human Rights in China report confirmed that individuals who appear to be linked to the Chinese state apparatus have been directly involved in attacks on Falun Gong and pro-Taiwan demonstrations in various cities over the last three decades.[85],[86] In May 2009, the US North Carolina State University buckled under pressure from a CI director and cancelled the Dalai Lama’s visit to its campus.[87] A former member of the Chinese Politburo Standing Committee, the CCP’s top leadership council, Li Changchun, openly acknowledged in 2009 that CIs were “an important part of China’s overseas propaganda setup.”[88]

The global backlash against such incidents led to CIs and CCs being shut down in several countries, whereupon China undertook strategic reforms to reshape its narrative and maintain its influence. In June 2020, it introduced two key measures: first, it shifted oversight of the global CC network to a new non-governmental organisation, the Chinese International Education Foundation; second, it renamed the former CI headquarters (Hanban) as the Centre for Language Education and Cooperation (CLEC), dissociating the government from CI funding.[89]

However, the measures do not seem to have made much difference to the global perception of CIs and CCs. In 2018, the US Congress restricted federal funding of Chinese language teaching for universities that already had CIs. Since then, the US Government Accountability Office reported in 2023 that nearly all the 100-odd CIs at US universities had been closed, though some were seeking alternative China-supported language programmes, thus continuing to raise oversight concerns of undue foreign influence.[90] By 2025, Australia had shuttered six university CIs,[91] while UK universities were re-evaluating CIs too.[92] In India as well, the 2020 Galwan clash triggered intense scrutiny of the seven CIs operating in the country, with the All India Council for Technical Education and University Grants Commission mandating that they would have to satisfy the preconditions of the Foreign Contribution (Regulation) Act to receive overseas funds.[93]

As China’s global clout increases, more Indians, in search of job opportunities, are learning Mandarin. This can be seen from the waiting list of Indian students seeking to take the Hanyu Shuiping Kaoshi (HSK), the test for Mandarin proficiency conducted by China’s Ministry of Education, at the single testing centre in Mumbai, India. Indeed, impatient Indians have been travelling to Lumbini in Nepal, which has another testing centre, to give the test; since April 2024, 50 percent of those taking the test in Lumbini have been Indians. HSK certification is a prerequisite for scholarships from the China Scholarship Council for further study of Mandarin in China. Thus, China’s educational outreach is quietly building familiarity and dependence, embedding Chinese cultural and institutional influence among young Indians.[94]

Chinese organisations coordinated by the UFWD systematically intervene in foreign universities to suppress academic freedom (relating to China) and propagate CCP ideology through a network comprising the CSSA, CIs, and supporting bodies. CSSA, the largest UFWD-controlled organisation for overseas Chinese students, ostensibly provides welfare support to students, but primarily monitors thoughts and behaviours, enforces pro-CCP speech, and harasses anti-China speakers. This has been repeatedly observed, instances including the CSSA-organised protest against a Dalai Lama speech at California University in June 2017; against a Chinese student’s speech at Maryland University in May 2017, which praised American democracy and freedom and criticised China’s authoritarian rule; at the counter protests following the demonstrations then Chinese Premier Li Keqiang faced from dissident Chinese on his visit to Australia in April 2017;at Canada’s McMaster University in February 2019, where a Uyghur activist’s lecture on re-education camps for the Muslim minority in Xinjiang province was reported by the CSSA to the Chinese consulate. Subsequently, in September 2019, McMaster University banned the CSSA for coordinating surveillance and intimidating pro-democracy students.

Even some Western publishers have begun obliging China. Cambridge University Press (CUP) and Springer Nature have censored content at the CCP’s request, restricting access to hundreds of academic articles for users in China. In August 2017, CUP initially removed over 300 papers relating to sensitive topics such as the Tiananmen Square protests of 1989 from The China Quarterly at the behest of China’s General Administration of Press and Publications, but restored them after severe backlash from Western scholars.[95] Springer Nature, however, continues to block over 1,000 titles, calling it a necessary trade-off for market access. In March 2025, Li Yanhe, a Taiwan-based publisher known for releasing works critical of Beijing, was arrested during his visit to mainland China and sentenced to three years for ‘inciting separatism.’ Such incidents underscore the ongoing challenges and pressures faced by publishers and authors in maintaining editorial independence while navigating the complexities of the Chinese market, demonstrating how market access considerations increasingly shape the boundaries of acceptable discourse on China.[96]

China systematically coerces multinational corporations (MNCs) into advancing its strategic objectives through market access weapons, economic sanctions, reputational threats, and social media attacks. There has been considerable pressure on them to represent Taiwan, Hong Kong, Tibet, and Macau as part of China on maps, company websites, and elsewhere. If companies refuse, China has even pressed for public apologies. In 2021, for instance, Swedish clothing brand H&M faced a coordinated backlash and consumer boycott in China after expressing concerns over alleged forced labour practices in Xinjiang.[97] In January 2018, Marriott International came under fire for listing Tibet, Taiwan, Hong Kong, and Macau as separate countries on a customer survey, prompting a swift apology and website correction.[98] That same year, leading US airlines were compelled to revise their online references to Taiwan, following demands from China. Fashion retailer Zara was pressured to issue a public apology in January 2018 for depicting Taiwan as a separate country on its website.[99] In early 2017, South Korean supermarket chain Lotte faced Chinese ire after Seoul installed US anti-missile systems on Lotte’s property, leading to the chain selling off its Chinese businesses and quitting the country. In April 2026, China imposed trade restrictions on seven European defence companies, including Belgium’s FN Browning and Germany’s Hensoldt AG, for allegedly supplying arms to Taiwan, banning exports of dual-use goods immediately.[100]

MNCs face pressure to support Chinese initiatives like the BRI and the China International Import Expo (CIIE) or risk market exclusion. Apple, with China as its third-largest market (after the US and Europe) and heavily reliant on China’s supply chain as well, has complied with the CCP guidebook, removing apps which crossed Chinese red lines, banning CCP-critical applications, and storing user data on government servers. Beijing’s calibrated control over digital religious spaces became all the more evident when the Pakistani-developed Quran Majeed app, reportedly used by nearly 40 million users globally, was removed from the Chinese variant of Apple’s App Store following regulatory objections by Chinese authorities.[101]

In the sporting world as well, China utilises the same tools to counter any messaging that goes against its interests. During the Hong Kong protests of 2019 over a proposed extradition law (which was later rescinded), Daryl Morey, general manager (GM) of Houston Rockets (one of the US’s National Basketball Association [NBA] teams) at the time, tweeted in support of the agitation.[102] When China responded with fury, the Rockets distanced themselves from their own GM, with LeBron James, one of the NBA’s best-known players who is also considered a social justice warrior,[103] criticising Morey, implying his comments were uninformed and harmful financially.[104] (However, NBA Commissioner Adam Silver backed Morey, despite the league losing revenue as a result.)[105] No NBA figure has since dared to criticise China publicly.

In the same year, Mesut Özil, then captain of the English Premier League team Arsenal, publicly denounced China’s treatment of Uyghurs in Xinjiang and the complicit silence of the international community.[106] Within days, the Premier League’s two broadcast partners in China, CCTV and PP Sports, refused to air an Arsenal match.[107] When they deigned to broadcast the matches later, the commentators refused to name Özil.[108] The following year, Özil was removed from the team, considering Arsenal’s business interests in China.[109]

Following Russia’s February 2022 invasion of Ukraine, widely condemned by the West, sporting associations such as Fédération Internationale de Football Association (FIFA) and the Union of European Football Associations (UEFA) have banned the country from participating in their sporting events.[110] China, allied to Russia in a ‘no-limits’ partnership, has not directly confronted these associations, but in 2022, it did halt broadcasts of English Premier League matches within the country.[111]

China’s quest for Pax Sinica has subtly evolved as a strategic global narrative war, wherein it embeds invisible sharp edges into its soft power. With its ingrained Tianxia worldview and pride of civilisation, its long-term objective is to shape international norms to align with its interests. Over the past two decades, this effort has shifted from regional diplomacy to a refined, multidomain, global-influencing operation. Unlike overt power plays, China operates via incremental influence silently embedding itself into the global media, international institutions, international sports, Western academia, Hollywood, and MNCs to assume an increasing control as its influence matures. Its values, including its authoritarian domestic rule, have been globally normalised by saturating cultural and intellectual spaces, making resistance to its narrative increasingly difficult.

Countries such as France, Canada, Italy, and South Africa have, in varying degrees, acknowledged China as the world’s top economy. Middle-income countries are doing the same as China invests heavily in their economies. In several African and Latin American countries, it is now being considered the chief ally.[112]

The Middle Kingdom has thus effectively amalgamated cultural diplomacy (soft power) with sharp power. Its CIs, scholarships, academic exchanges, and participation in sports are instruments of the former which in turn bolster the latter through tactics such as campaigning against the Dalai Lama’s international visits, banning select sporting figures on domestic media, or seeking media censorship through economic coercion.

The more Chinese narratives take root globally, the more amenable the world may become to its geopolitical ambitions. The subtle nature of its strategy makes it particularly difficult to contest, as influence exercised without overt coercion is often normalised without significant scrutiny. China is poised to further sharpen its soft-power tools through technological advancements, strategic alliances, and ideological messaging. To counter surging Chinese soft power, preserve institutional independence, safeguard democratic discourse, and maintain a balanced multipolar international order, the world needs to strengthen its media, institutional safeguards, and transparency mechanisms, and keep an eye on the evolving Chinese strategy.
